items.title: Unlimited Free GLM-5.3 Coder (100M Free Tokens!): This is ACTUALLY REALLY FREE!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about the new GLM-5.3 ZCode Weekend Build event, where Z AI is giving new users 100 million free GLM-5.3 tokens to use inside ZCode for a limited time.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Z AI has brought back the GLM-5.3 ZCode Weekend Build event with 50,000 free token packs.
🎁 New ZCode users can get 100 million free GLM-5.3 tokens with no credit card or claiming required.
⏳ The event runs from August 21 to August 23 Pacific time, and unused tokens expire when the event ends.
💻 The free tokens only work inside the ZCode desktop app, not through APIs, Claude Code, Cline, or other tools.
🧠 GLM-5.3 is a security-specialized coding model with strong performance in code auditing and vulnerability discovery.
📊 GLM-5.3 scored 73 out of 80 on my benchmark, beating several major coding models.
🛠️ ZCode includes project indexing, MCP servers, Goal Mode, Git integration, browser automation, and built-in previews.
💸 Even after the event, ZCode still offers a 5-day free trial
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, GLM53 just came out and I already made a video on it where I ran it through my own bench and it ended up at number one. If you missed that one, it will be linked below. But today, I am not here to talk about benchmarks. I am here because ZAI is basically giving the model away for free right now. And there is a very specific reason I am only making this video now instead of last week. So, let's get right into it. About a week ago, ZAI announced something called the GLM53 times Zcode weekend build. The deal was that if you were a new user and you logged into Zcode for the first time during the window, you would automatically get 100 million free GLM53 tokens. No claiming, no credit card, nothing. Just log in and it lands in your account. And I was going to cover it. I had the script halfwritten, but it died in about an hour. ZI's own words were that demand exceeded expectations and service capacity was being adjusted. So roughly 60 minutes after it went live, they pulled it. Anyone who signed up during that hour kept their tokens, but everyone after that just got the normal 3 million token trial instead. So I did not film it. There was no point telling you about a free offer that no longer existed. But it is now back. Round two is live. And this time they have actually put a number on it. 50,000 packs, first come, first served. And the window is bigger. It runs from August 21 at 9:00 a.m. Pacific to August 23 at 6:00 p.m. Pacific. Let me convert that because Pacific is not useful for everyone. On Eastern time, that is noon on August 24. In India, it is 9:30 p.m. on August 24. And in UTC + 8, which is what ZAI's own announcement uses, it is midnight on August 23 through 9:00 a.m. on August 24th. So that is roughly 2 1/2 days. And as I'm recording this, we are already inside the window, which means if you want this, do it now and not after the video ends. 50,000 spots sounds like a lot, but the last round burned through its capacity in an hour, so I would not gamble on it lasting. Now, a few conditions you should know. First, it is new users only. If you already made a Zcode account back when I covered GLM 5.2 on it, you are almost certainly not eligible. And from what I can tell, if you have an active coding plan, you are also not eligible. Second, it is Zcode only. You cannot take these tokens and pipe them into Claude code or Klein or your own scripts through the API. You have to use the actual Zcode app. And third, this is the important one. Unused tokens expire when the event ends. This is not a 100 million token balance that sits in your account forever. If you sign up and then do nothing until next Tuesday, you get nothing out of it. And you can actually see that in the app. It shows up as a start plan with an expiry date on it and then a today's balance section with GLM5 Tour 3 and GLM5 Turbo sitting at 100% resetting at 2359 each day. So it behaves like a very large daily allowance across the event window, not one giant lump sum you slowly chip away at. Which means the play here is simple. Sign up and then actually use it today. Now let me put these numbers into perspective because token counts get thrown around so much that they stop meaning anything. The normal free trial on Zcode gives new users about 3 million tokens per day for GLM 5.3 plus another 2 million for GLM 5 Turbo running for 5 days. So the standard trial is roughly 15 million tokens of the main model in total. This event is giving you 100 million. That is around 6 to 7 times the entire standard trial. And with a coding agent, tokens do go fast, but not that fast. For a normal person building normal projects, 100 million tokens across a weekend is effectively unlimited. You would have to be running long horizon agent tasks back to back on a huge repo for hours on end to meaningfully dent that. So this is a genuinely free weekend with a Frontier level model and I do not say that lightly. Now let's talk about the model itself quickly. For anyone who has not seen my other video, GLM 5.3 is the same parameter count and the same architecture as GLM 5.2. 2. It is not a new base model. It is 5.2 post-trained much further. Now, let's talk about Zcode because you have to use it to get this deal. Zcode is ZAI's own agentic development environment. It is not a chat UI and it is not a VS code fork. It is a desktop app built specifically around GLM. So, instead of forcing GLM into a harness that was designed around Claude, you are using it in the thing that was actually built for it. It has project indexing, skills, MCP servers, custom commands, usage tracking, a built-in preview with dev tools, git integration, browser automation, and goal mode. Goal mode is the one I would actually use for this weekend. It keeps the agent focused on a larger objective, creates a task list, tracks progress, uses the readonly explore sub agent for investigation, and just works until the goal is done or it is genuinely blocked. That is the mode where a big token grant actually matters. There is also a remote angle now. You can control Zcode from your phone. And there are bots for WeChat, FU, and Telegram. So you can kick off a long task and check on it from somewhere else. It runs on Mac OS, both Apple Silicon and Intel, Windows on 64-bit, and ARM and Linux as debone is covered. One thing it still does not have is custom userdefined sub aents. You get the built-in explore sub agent, which is readon and useful. But if you want Verdant style multi-agent orchestration, that is not here yet. Now, here is the part I actually want you to pay attention to. The event ends, but the free tier does not after this weekend. Zcode still gives new users that 5-day trial with 3 million tokens per day on GLM 5.3 and 2 million on GLM 5 Turbo. That is the same fallback everyone got when the first round was suspended, and it is still live. So, even if the 50,000 packs run out before you get to it, you have not missed everything. 3 million tokens a day is enough to build real things. And if you do decide to pay after that, the coding plan is still one of the better deals in this space. Light is $18 a month, pro is 72, and max is 160. There is currently a promo that knocks those down to roughly 1260, 50.40, and 112 on light. You are looking at around 80 prompts per 5 hours and about 400 per week. Pro is roughly five times that. max is around 20 times that. There is also a 1.5 times quota boost running through August 31, which is that 150% quotota badge you see inside the app. That stacks with everything else. And a trick most people miss, off- peak calls cost half the points. Peak hours are 2:00 p.m. to 6 p.m. in UTC plus 8 on weekdays only. So if you do your heavy agent work outside that window, which for most of us in the West is basically always, you effectively double your quota for free. Nobody tells you this, but it is right there in the docs. Oh, and Zai says the weights are going up on Hugging Face roughly 2 weeks after launch. So, if you have the hardware or you want to run it through some other provider later, that door opens, too. Now, my honest advice for this weekend, do not waste it on toy prompts. Do not sign up, type, make me a snake game, watch it work, go, "Okay, that is pretty cool." And then close the app. You will have burned a 100 million token grant on nothing. And remember, it expires when the event does. Use it on something real, a bug tracker, a small CRM, a dashboard for something you actually track, a content calendar, or take an existing repo of yours, point it at the codebase, and ask it to audit for vulnerabilities, since that is literally what this model was specialized for. That is the one test where GLM 5.3 does something the other models do not do as well. And use the loop properly. Explore first, then plan, then build, then verify. Do not just throw one giant wish into the chat and hope. I covered the full workflow for this in my GLM 5.2 Zcode video and all of it still applies. So check that one out if you want the whole setup with skills and MCPs. One last thing, it is a free tier. So use some judgment. Do not throw private company code, secrets, or customer data at a free promotional endpoint unless you have read the data policy and you're okay with it. Personal projects, open source projects, test repos, side projects, that is what this is for. Free is great. leaking your company source code is not great. Anyway, the first round of this lasted about an hour before it collapsed under its own demand, which should tell you something about how many people want to try this model. Round two has a hard cap of 50,000 packs, and it is running right now. So, if you have been curious about GLM 5.3, this is the cheapest possible way to find out whether it works for you. The link is in the description. Go grab it before the spots are gone and then actually use the thing. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Ox Alpha (Fully Tested) : So, This is GLM-5.5?! IT'S CRAZY!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about Delta, Zed’s new AI agent GUI, which uses DeltaDB to make agent conversations, code changes, and version history fully connected and traceable.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Zed has launched Delta, a standalone AI agent GUI built around coding through threaded conversations.
🧠 Delta runs on DeltaDB, a new version control layer that records every operation between commits.

items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So, there's a new stealth model in town and it's called Ox Alpha. It just dropped on Open Code as an anonymous model and nobody knows which provider it's from. Open Code is saying that it's free for the next week and it comes with a 1 million token context window, multimodal support, and zero data retention. They're also saying that they have capacity for 100 trillion tokens per day, which is just insane. So, you can basically use it as much as you want right now. Now, whenever a stealth model drops like this, the whole community goes into detective mode, and this time is no different. People are speculating that it's a new model from GLM. I cannot confirm this because there's no official confirmation for it. So, take it with a grain of salt, but the evidence is quite interesting, and we'll talk about that in a bit. First, let's talk about how it actually performs because I have tested it on my king bench and the results are pretty crazy. So on Kingbench, Ox Alpha scored 70 out of 80, which is 87.5%. That puts it in second place on my entire leaderboard, just behind GLM 5.3, which sits at 91.25%. It's ahead of Fable 5 at 82.5%, Quen 3.8 Max at 81.25% and even Opus 4.8 at 80%. So this thing is beating almost every Frontier model out there, which is just amazing. for a random stealth model. If we look at the individual tests, it got a perfect 10 on the 3JS contact lens case, the Panda SVG, the hard maths permutation question, and the Gemma FinTuning task. The finetuning one is especially impressive because most models completely fall apart on that. It also did well on the elevator simulation and the bow and arrow game with 8S on both. The only places where it dropped some points were the folding table and the 3D wrist clock where it got sevens. But to be honest, the risk clock question destroys almost every model anyway. So a seven there is actually one of the best scores on that question. So this is kind of great. But it's not just my benchmark. Ben Davis also ran it through 10 tasks on Deep SWA and the results there are even more interesting. Ox Alpha scored 80% on that subset and he said it was a near miss on the failed ones. So it's actually a bit above 80%. For comparison, Fable 5 got 65%. GLM 5.3 got 62%, Grock 46 got 62% and GPT 5.6 Soul only got 52%. It even solved the Marriott task in a single shot where GLM 5.3, GPT 5.6 Soul, and Groc 4.6 all went zero out of four. Now, he does mention that it's only a 10 task subset, so there could be a ton of variance in the real score, but still beating everything else by 15 points on the same subset is quite great to see. Anyway, now let's come to the big question. Who made this thing? Ben Davis actually put out a full writeup investigating exactly this, and it'll be linked below. His conclusion is that it's most likely JIEP's next generation unified multimodal GLM, and he's putting around 90% confidence on that. His strongest evidence comes from video encoder fingerprinting. He ran controlled video tests, and OX Alpha's token counts matched GLM 5V Turbo exactly across every scenario. same FPS in variant frame sampling, same duration scaling at around 147 tokens per second, and the same per frame resolution scaling. Other providers showed completely different signatures. On top of that, the tokenizer counts matched GLM 5.3 exactly across 25 different prompts, which basically requires an identical vocabulary. The writing style also matches with the emoji decorated responses that GLM and QN models are known for. And just like GLM 5V, it rejects audio input, which rules out models like MIMO that actually support audio. He also systematically ruled out DeepSeek, Qen, Xiaomi, and the Western Labs based on these fingerprints. I am saying most likely because none of this is official confirmation. It could be that some of these signals are misleading, and we won't know for sure until the reveal. But this is also the fifth stealth release in this series, and every previous one was claimed by a Chinese lab at reveal. The free period ends around the 27th of August. So, we should find out pretty soon. Now, here's the interesting part if you ask me. On my bench, Ox Alpha actually scored a bit below GLM 5.3, but on Deep SWU, it scored way above it. So, if this really is a GLM model, it seems to be a stronger checkpoint that's more tuned for agentic coding work rather than oneshot generation. That would make sense if it's their next generation model rather than just a variant. Overall, this model is pretty amazing to be honest. It's free right now. It has a 1 million token context and is putting up frontier level numbers on multiple benchmarks. If the GLM speculation turns out to be true and they price it like their previous models, then this could be a really good option for sure. The Western labs should honestly be a bit worried because open weight or not, the Chinese labs are now trading blows at the very top. I'd say go try it out while it's free and form your own opinion on it. I'll be doing more testing on it as well, and if the reveal happens, I'll cover that, too. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the [music] super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this [music] video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [bell]

In this video, I'll be telling you about Delta, Zed's new AI agent app built around conversation-first coding, collaborative threads, and a new version control layer called DeltaDB that connects every code change back to the agent conversation that created it.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Zed has launched Delta, a standalone AI agent GUI focused on coding through threads instead of a traditional editor-first workflow.
🧠 Delta runs on DeltaDB, a new version control layer that records operations between commits and links code changes directly to conversations.
🤝 Delta supports multiplayer collaboration, allowing teammates and agents to join the same thread, comment, co-edit prompts, and continue work together.
🌐 A browser version is available at Delta dot dev, using the same Rust app compiled to WebAssembly, so you can try it without installing anything.
🔑 Delta supports Zed-hosted models, ChatGPT Plus and Pro sign-in, API keys for multiple providers, and GitHub Copilot integration.
🛠️ Agents c
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Zed has launched a new app called Delta, and I got early access to it. So, I really wanted to talk about this one. Delta is basically Zed's entry into AI agent GUIs. It's a standalone app, separate from the Zed editor, and it's built around the idea that you code by talking to agents in threads, instead of living in an editor with a chat panel bolted on the side. But, the real twist here is what's underneath it. Delta runs on DeltaDB, which is Zed's new version control layer that they've been teasing for a while. Git captures snapshots when you commit, but DeltaDB records every operation that happens in between commits, gives each one a stable identity, and links every change to the conversation that produced it. So, from any line of code, you can find the exact agent conversation that shaped it, and from any conversation, you can jump to the code it produced. Zed's whole pitch is that the conversation between you and an agent is the actual source of your software, and your tooling should treat it that way, which is a pretty interesting way to think about it, to be honest. It's also multiplayer. It uses CRDTs under the hood, so multiple people and agents can be in the same thread at the same time, and teammates can join via a link to comment, co-edit prompts, or continue the work. There's also a browser version at delta.dev, which is the same Rust app compiled to WebAssembly, so nothing needs to be installed, and it stays compatible with your existing Git repositories, so your teammates who don't use Delta won't even notice anything different. Now, let me show you my demo of it and how it works. So, this is the Delta app. As you can see, it's not really an editor at first glance. There's a sidebar with your projects and threads, and the main area is just a thread. I have a small movie tracker project added here, which is just a fresh Next.js scaffold. Let me start by asking, what is this project about? Once I send it, you can see it starts working. The thread also automatically renames itself to movie tracker project overview, which is a nice touch. You can see it loads a skill called using superpowers, then it lists the directory and reads the readme, the package.json, and the claw.md files. It thinks in between as well, and it noticed that the readme is still the default scaffold, so it went ahead and checked the actual application code, too. Then it gives me a proper project summary. It says it's a newly created Next.js 16 project with React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind named Movie Tracker. But the actual product functionality has not been built yet, which is correct. At the bottom, you can see the status bar. It shows the project and the branch, and on the right, you can see the model, which is 5.6 sol for me, along with the effort level set to medium. I'm on the VIP plan here, which is their early access subscription thing. There's also a share button at the top. If I click it, it starts preparing the thread for sharing, and you can send that link to a teammate, and they can join the thread, look through the whole history, and even talk to the same agent that did the work. Since this is all backed by Delta DB, the thread is not just a chat log. It's basically the version history itself. Now, let's take a quick look at the settings. In the LLM provider section, you can see I have access hosted models through the subscription, and there are 24 models shown in the model picker. But here's the part I really like. You can sign in with your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription to use OpenAI models in Delta. You can also plug in your own API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, and Base10, and there's a GitHub Copilot sign-in option as well. So, you are not locked into their subscription, which is quite great to see. There are also appearance settings with light and dark modes, and you can even choose the diff colors and diff markers. Then there are pane settings for line numbers, soft wrap, and the default diff base, and some thread settings as well. And even though it's conversation first, there is a real editor in here. If I open the file tree and click on a file, it opens the code in a proper editor pane with syntax highlighting. So, you can always look at the actual code side by side with the thread. Now, let's give it some real work. I'll just say, "Do some edits and make it faster." This is where it gets interesting. It starts thinking, loads a brainstorming skill, and runs some Git commands to check the state of the repo. But, instead of just charging ahead, it comes back and says the project is still an untouched scaffold. So, make it faster could mean different things, and it gives me three options. A is the recommended one, which is to build a polished lightweight movie tracker homepage while keeping JavaScript minimal. B is a full MVP with search and watch lists. C is performance only. I'll just reply with A. Then, it asks another question about what the homepage should actually do, again with three options. I'll pick A again, which is a cinematic landing page with curated sample movies. And then, it does something I haven't seen before. It offers to open a browser tab and put together mock-ups and comparisons as we go. But, it warns me that it's still new and can be token intensive, and asks if I want it. I'll just say, "Just build it, please. No more questions." So, now it gets to work. And you can see it works in a very structured way. First, it writes a full design spec into a docs folder and commits it. You can see the commit happening right in the thread, and it shows up as external changes with the commit hash in the movie tracker repo. Then, it loads a writing plan skill, and writes an implementation plan, which is a proper 184-line document, and commits that as well. After that, it loads an executing plan skill along with a Git work tree skill, and this part is pretty cool. It runs within an agent-specific isolated clone. If you look at the paths, it's working inside a dot-delta-clones folder. So, the agent gets its own isolated copy of the repo, and spinning these up is basically free because Delta DB virtualizes the work tree. That means agents can go wild on branches without stepping on your working directory. Then, it runs npm install and npm run lint to verify the baseline. It even digs into the Next.js 16 docs that are bundled inside node modules to check the current guidance for fonts, metadata, and server and client components before it changes anything. And it writes tests first. You can see it creating a test contract with things like the landing page exposes semantic landmarks, the layout has product metadata, and styles respect reduced motion preferences. It patches the package.json to add the test script and commits the test contract before writing the actual page. Then it starts building the actual landing page. It writes a server-rendered page with a curated movies array, a proper header, hero section, watchlist section, and footer. And then it goes all-in on a CSS-only cinematic design system. Feature cards with rotations and shadows, gradients, hand-drawn style artwork done purely in CSS, all with zero client-side JavaScript and zero image requests. And the whole time, every step lands as a commit, and each commit shows up in the thread as external changes. So, the thread and the repo history are basically the same thing, which is the whole Delta DB idea in action. >> If I click the branch switcher at the bottom, you can see the main branch along with the work tree branches that the agent created. You also get options to view files, copy the project path, and copy the branch name from here. So, this is kind of great. It asks before doing ambiguous things. It plans and commits like a disciplined engineer, and everything stays traceable back to the conversation. Now, a few more things worth mentioning. Claude code is also integrated. Your terminal sessions can sync live into Delta threads through ACP, the agent client protocol, which is the same protocol Zed built for their editor integrations. I have a video on that as well, which will be linked below. There are also cloud runners, so agents can keep working even after you close your laptop, and the conversation stays synchronized when you come back. As for pricing, they haven't announced anything for Delta yet. It's in early access right now with invites rolling out, and you can sign up on their site with your email and GitHub username. Zed has also said they plan to open source Delta DB with optional paid services and eventually bring it into the main Zed editor as well, which is quite great because Zed open sourcing their stuff is one of the reasons I like them. If you ask me, this is one of the more interesting takes on AI coding tools I've seen recently. Everyone else is building agent GUIs that are basically chat plus a diff viewer, but Zed went one level deeper and rebuilt the version control layer so that agent work is actually traceable. Whether people are ready to move their workflow into threads instead of editors is another question and it's still early access, so take it with a grain of salt, but the foundation here is really solid. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video [music] a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
